passage: Vaibhav had wanted a motorbike since he started driving the tractor on his uncle's farm outside Satara. The dealer in town smiled and said, "Zero down payment, small EMI, sign here." Jyoti, his cousin who kept accounts for the dairy co-op, asked to see the paper first. She sat on the dealer's bench with a pencil and added up the monthly payments for three years. The total was much more than the bike's price. "The EMI is small because it runs long," she said. "And if you miss one, there's a late charge on top." Vaibhav stared at the figure. He had planned only for the monthly amount. He didn't sign that day. He went home to count what he could put down first.

qa.q: Who added up the monthly payments?
qa.a: Jyoti, his cousin who keeps accounts for the dairy co-op, added them up.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav realise when he saw Jyoti's total?
qa.a: He realised he had only thought about the monthly amount and had not understood how much more the loan would cost overall.

qa.q: What went well in how Vaibhav handled the offer?
qa.a: He let someone check the paper and did not sign on the spot, giving himself time to think about saving first.

qa.q: How might the dealer see Vaibhav walking away?
qa.a: The dealer may see a lost sale, since the easy offer depended on buyers looking only at the small monthly payment.

grounding: Shows a young man learning that a small EMI over a long period adds up to much more than the price.

passage: Dalia got her first credit card in her second year at university in Valencia. The statement came with a line in bold: minimum payment due. It was tiny, so she paid it and felt responsible. Three months later her balance had barely moved. She showed Xin, her flatmate, who studied economics. Xin pointed at a smaller line she'd skipped: the interest charged. "You're paying mostly interest," Xin said. "The rest keeps growing on itself." Dalia felt a hot rush of embarrassment. She cut the card up that night, which Xin said was one way, and taped the statement to her wardrobe door. She decided to ask the student money advice office what her options were.

qa.q: What was printed in bold on Dalia's statement?
qa.a: The minimum payment due was printed in bold.

qa.q: How did Dalia feel when Xin explained the interest, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, described as a hot rush, because she had believed paying the minimum was responsible.

qa.q: What sensible next step did Dalia take?
qa.a: She planned to ask the student money advice office about her options instead of guessing alone.

qa.q: What would change if Dalia had read the interest line from the start?
qa.a: She would have seen early that the minimum barely touched her balance and could have changed course sooner.

grounding: Shows a student discovering how credit card interest compounds when only the minimum is paid.

passage: In the hostel common room, Eshaan kept refreshing his phone. Jomon, a senior who helped run the hostel's money-awareness evenings, noticed his leg bouncing. "Everything okay?" Eshaan showed him a message from an instant loan app: pay today or they would contact his contacts. He had borrowed a little for fees, then more to repay the first loan. "It kept growing," he said quietly. Jomon didn't lecture. He said threats like that were a known pattern and that Eshaan should not borrow again to cover it. He walked him to the warden's office and helped him find the college's student support cell. Eshaan's shoulders dropped a little as he wrote down the timing. "I thought I was the only one," he said.

qa.q: Why had Eshaan first borrowed money from the app?
qa.a: He borrowed a little to pay fees.

qa.q: What does Eshaan's bouncing leg and quiet voice suggest?
qa.a: They suggest he was anxious and ashamed about the debt and the threatening messages.

qa.q: How did Jomon support Eshaan well?
qa.a: He stayed calm, did not lecture, and took him to the warden and the student support cell so trusted people could help.

qa.q: How might Eshaan's family see the situation if he had kept hiding it?
qa.a: They might only learn about it through the lender's threats, which would likely feel far more frightening than hearing it from him first. 🫂

grounding: Shows a student caught in a growing debt cycle from borrowing to repay loans, and being guided to trusted help.

passage:
Hey Eshaan,
You said you're getting your first credit card next month, so let me tell you what happened to me. Last year I bought a phone on my card and paid only the 'minimum due' each month because it seemed small. I thought I was fine. Then I actually read the statement. Interest was being charged on the whole unpaid balance, and the next month on that interest too. After eight months I owed more than the phone had cost, even though I had paid every single month. I felt stupid and scared. I told Appa, which was awful, and we sat with the statement to understand it and make a plan to clear it. So read the statement, understand how the interest works before you swipe, and if something doesn't add up, ask someone you trust or the bank. Don't be me.
Chinmay

qa.q: What did Chinmay buy on the card?
qa.a: A phone.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel when Chinmay finally read the statement?
qa.a: Stupid and scared, because Chinmay owed more than the phone cost despite paying every month.

qa.q: What does Chinmay want Eshaan to do before using a credit card?
qa.a: Read the statement, understand how interest builds on an unpaid balance, and ask a trusted person or the bank if something does not add up.

qa.q: How might Appa have felt when Chinmay told him?
qa.a: Probably worried and maybe disappointed, but willing to sit with Chinmay and make a plan, which shows care.

grounding: An email shows a young adult explaining from experience how card interest compounds when only the minimum is paid.

passage: Sachin, you asked why I freaked out when you mentioned that instant loan app. Okay, story time. In second year I needed money for a laptop repair before exams. An app offered 'instant approval, no paperwork'. I tapped yes in five minutes. What I didn't read: a big processing fee cut from the amount, and a charge for every day I was late. I missed one due date by a week, and suddenly the total was almost double. Then they started calling my contacts. That was the worst part, my aunt getting a call saying 'Kashish has unpaid dues'. I was shaking. My mother helped me pay it off, and a lawyer friend of hers helped us report the harassment. Now I read every loan term twice: interest, fees, late charges. If it's instant and easy, I get suspicious.

qa.q: What did Kashish need the money for?
qa.a: A laptop repair before exams.

qa.q: What was the worst part for Kashish, and how did it feel?
qa.a: The app calling Kashish's contacts, including the aunt; Kashish was left shaking and ashamed.

qa.q: What does Kashish do now when a loan offer appears?
qa.a: Kashish reads every term twice, especially interest, fees and late charges, and treats 'instant and easy' as a warning sign.

qa.q: How might Kashish's aunt have felt getting that call?
qa.a: Surprised and worried, and perhaps embarrassed on Kashish's behalf.

grounding: A young adult tells a friend how a quick loan with hidden fees became a debt trap and how they got out with help.
